summaries.example: Imagine a map with several places. The letter p might mean “it is raining,” and that can be true in more than one place. The letter a can name one special place. The formula @_a p means “at the place named a, it is raining.” A satisfaction operator such as @_a lets us check a statement at that named place, even when we start somewhere else on the map.
summaries.summary: Hybrid logic is an expanded form of modal logic. Modal logic studies statements whose truth can depend on a possible world, a time, or another point. For example, “it is raining” may be true at one time and false at another. But ordinary modal logic is not designed to name one exact point, such as a particular time. Hybrid logic adds nominals, special symbols that are true at exactly one point. A nominal can therefore act like a name. It also adds satisfaction operators. A formula such as @_a p says that p is true at the point named a. Hybrid logic can include binders too. One binder can consider different points, while another attaches a name to the point currently being examined. These tools give the logic more expressive power: they allow it to state things about particular points and compare them. The subject also includes precise meanings for these symbols, translations between hybrid logic and first-order logic, systems of axioms, proof methods, decision procedures, and versions that discuss time, knowledge, computer states, or other structures. Its history reaches back to Arthur N. Prior’s work on tense logic.
key_ideas: Ordinary modal logic can describe things that change from one world, time, or state to another.
Hybrid logic adds nominals, which name one particular point.
Satisfaction operators let us ask whether something is true at a named point.
Some hybrid systems use binders to name the current point or to consider all points.
Hybrid logic can describe certain patterns, such as whether a point can lead back to itself.
Researchers study its meanings, translations, rules for proving things, and computer procedures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hybrid logic gives us a careful way to talk about both general possibilities and specific places in a structure. That can help when studying time, possible situations, computer systems, information, and knowledge. It also shows how adding a small new kind of symbol can make a logic express things that the older system could not express.

important_terms.definition: A kind of logic that adds special tools to modal logic so it can talk about particular worlds, times, or states.
A point or world where a statement is being checked. It might represent a time, a possible world, or a computer state.
A special symbol that is true at exactly one point. It works like a name for that point.
An operator that checks whether a formula is true at the point named by a nominal.
A rule or symbol that connects a statement with points, such as checking every possible point.
A relation that tells us which points can be reached from another point.

questions_to_think_about: Why might naming one exact time be more useful than merely saying what happens at different times?
What could a named point represent in a computer program?
If two names point to the same place, what should happen when we compare them?
Would a map be easier or harder to use if every place had a special name?

summaries.example: Let worlds be computer states, with wRv meaning that state v can occur in one step from state w. Let c name the current state and let p mean “the system is safe.” Then @_c p says that the system is safe at the state named c. The hybrid formula c → □¬c says that no state named c has a transition to itself; it expresses irreflexivity. This illustrates the difference between merely describing accessible states and referring to one particular state.
summaries.summary: Hybrid logic extends ordinary modal logic by adding symbols that refer to individual points in a Kripke-style structure. In modal semantics, a point may represent a possible world, time, epistemic state, or computer state, and ordinary propositional symbols can have different truth-values at different points. A nominal is different: it is true at exactly one point and can therefore function as a name. With satisfaction operators, @_a φ means that φ holds at the point named by a, not necessarily at the point where evaluation began. This makes it possible to express reference and identity; for instance, @_a b says that the points named by a and b coincide. Hybrid languages may also include binders. The universal binder varies a nominal over points, while the downarrow binder assigns a nominal to the current point. The latter is definable using the former in the basic setting described by the entry. Formally, hybrid models retain worlds, an accessibility relation, and valuations, while assignments map nominals to worlds. The entry explains validity and truth conditions, and shows that hybrid formulas can describe frame features such as irreflexivity that ordinary modal formulas cannot. It also develops translations to first-order logic with equality and back from relevant first-order fragments. Historically, the approach grows from Arthur N. Prior’s hybrid tense logic, where forward and backward operators describe temporal direction. Later work developed axioms, analytic proof methods, decision procedures, quantified systems, and applications. The entry also notes a philosophical question about whether hybrid formulations and first-order formulations have the same ontological commitments, even when they have the same expressive power.
key_ideas: Modal logic evaluates formulas at points, while hybrid logic also gives names to individual points.
Nominals and satisfaction operators can express reference and identity; @_a b can say that two nominals designate the same point.
The downarrow binder names the current point, and the universal binder ranges a nominal over points. The downarrow binder can be defined using the universal binder.
Hybrid logic translates into first-order logic with equality, and important fragments of first-order logic translate back into hybrid logic.
Hybrid formulas can express frame properties such as irreflexivity, asymmetry, antisymmetry, and universality that ordinary modal logic cannot express in a single formula.

The field includes axiomatic systems, tableaux, Gentzen and natural-deduction systems, decision procedures, quantified versions, and applications to time, computing, knowledge representation, and structured data.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hybrid logic clarifies the difference between describing how truth varies across points and referring to a particular point. That distinction matters in philosophical accounts of time and modality, and it is useful in formal descriptions of computational systems, information, knowledge, and structured digital data. The subject also connects semantics with proof theory: researchers investigate when formulas are valid, how proofs can be constructed, whether satisfiability can be decided, and how these results change when binders or quantifiers are added.

important_terms.definition: A modal logic enriched with devices for referring to individual points in its semantic structure.
A special propositional symbol interpreted as true at exactly one world or point; it functions like a name for that point.
The point, world, time, or state at which a formula is evaluated.
An expression @_a φ stating that φ is true at the point assigned to nominal a, regardless of the starting point of evaluation.
A symbol that changes how a nominal is assigned: ∀ ranges over points, while ↓ assigns a nominal to the current point.
A structure consisting of points and a relation specifying which points are accessible from which others.
A formula true in every model based on a particular frame, or in every frame when no class is specified.
The property of being expressible by formulas of a given logic. Hybridization can increase expressive power without necessarily increasing decision complexity in the same way.

questions_to_think_about: Does giving a point a name change only what a language can say, or also what the points are?
Why might a satisfaction operator be useful when the formula is evaluated at a different point?
What is gained, and what philosophical concern might arise, when a nominal is treated like a first-order term?
How can a translation preserve truth while changing from hybrid notation to first-order notation?
Why might researchers want proof systems that work uniformly across many modal logics?

summaries.example: Suppose a story has several moments: before a storm, during the storm, and after it. The ordinary symbol p might mean “the streets are wet,” so p can be true at some moments and false at others. A nominal a can name the exact moment “during the storm.” Then @_a p means “the streets are wet during the moment named a.” If b names the same moment, @_a b is true; if b names another moment, it is false. Hybrid logic can therefore discuss both changing facts and particular moments.
summaries.summary: Hybrid logic is modal logic supplemented with a way to refer to individual points. Modal semantics evaluates formulas at points connected by an accessibility relation. Depending on the application, these points may be possible worlds, times, epistemic states, or states of a computer. An ordinary proposition can vary in truth from point to point, but it does not by itself identify one exact point. A nominal fills that role: it is interpreted as true at exactly one point. Satisfaction operators add another important ability. In @_a φ, the nominal a directs evaluation to its designated point, and φ is tested there. Consequently, @_a b can express that the points named by a and b are identical. Hybrid languages can also contain binders. The ∀ binder considers alternative assignments of a nominal across points, while ↓ binds a nominal to the point currently under evaluation. The entry gives formal semantics using models, assignments, valuations, and frames, then explains validity and the relation between hybrid and first-order reasoning. It presents translations from hybrid logic into first-order logic with equality, and translations back for appropriate fragments. These results illuminate both the power and the limits of the different formalisms. In tense logic, associated with Arthur N. Prior, the points are moments and two operators look forward and backward along the temporal relation. The history after Prior includes work on axioms, pure formulas, proof systems, tableaux, model checking, complexity, quantified hybrid logic, and applications in areas such as artificial intelligence, specification, and structured data. key_ideas: Modal logic handles truth that depends on a point, such as a time or possible world, but ordinary propositions do not name exact points.
Nominals add names for individual points, and satisfaction operators allow a formula to be checked at a named point.
Hybrid logic can express that two names refer to the same point and can describe structural properties such as irreflexivity and universality.
The universal binder ranges over possible assignments to a nominal; the downarrow binder makes a nominal refer to the current point.

Hybrid logic has close connections with first-order logic with equality. The full basic system described can match its expressive power, while a weaker binder-free system corresponds to a bounded fragment.
Arthur N. Prior’s tense logic helped inspire the field. Later research developed axioms, tableaux, natural deduction, decision procedures, quantified systems, and applications.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hybrid logic is important because it combines two useful perspectives: general movement among possibilities and precise reference to one selected point. This combination supports formal analysis of time, modality, knowledge, computer processes, and information structures. It also provides a meeting place for semantics, proof theory, and computation. Studying it reveals how a language’s vocabulary affects what can be expressed, how formulas can be translated, and how questions about meaning may remain distinct from purely technical equivalence.

important_terms.definition: A system that expands modal logic with symbols for referring to single worlds, times, or states.
A special propositional symbol that is true at one point only, so it can serve as a name for that point.
A formal device that evaluates a formula at the point named by a nominal.
An expression that assigns or ranges over names for points. The main binders discussed are ∀ and ↓.
A set of points together with a relation showing which points are accessible from each point.
A mapping that gives ordinary propositional symbols their truth-values at points.
A formula’s ability to describe structures or properties that another logic cannot describe.
A method of translating formulas between two logical languages while preserving whether they are true.

questions_to_think_about: Why is “it is raining” different, logically, from “it is noon on one particular date”?
What does @_a φ add that simply writing φ at the current point does not?
Why might two systems have similar expressive power but different philosophical interpretations?
How do the forward and backward operators in tense logic represent different temporal directions?
Why could a logic become more expressive without becoming equally harder to decide?
